usage: I wash my hands with soap.
비누 ends in a vowel, so the means particle is 로 (not 으로)
거품 = bubbles/foam; the lather you work up before rinsing
The soap is all worn down.
닳다 = to wear away; the natural verb for a bar shrinking with use
a flat bar is counted with 장; a boxed/whole one can also be 개
examples: 손에 비누를 묻혀요.
I put soap on my hands.
simple: 묻히다 = to get/apply something onto a surface
비누로 손을 깨끗이 씻어요.
I wash my hands clean with soap.
everyday: 로 marks the tool you wash WITH, and 을 marks the hands you wash
이 비누는 향이 순해서 아기도 써요.
This soap has a mild scent so even the baby uses it.
real-situation: 향이 순하다 (the scent is mild) is the natural review phrase
nuance: 비누 is solid BAR soap for hands or body, and it pairs almost automatically with 씻다 (wash) and 거품을 내다 (work up a lather). The key contrast for a shopper is form, not meaning: liquid body cleanser is 바디워시, hand pump soap is 핸드워시/물비누, and a facial cleanser is 클렌저 or 폼클렌징 — calling all of these 비누 sounds like you mean a hard bar. Note 비누 is a native Korean word with no hanja, so do not try to break it into characters. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: you wash WITH soap, so it must be 비누로 손을 씻다 (instrument), never 비누를 씻다, which would literally mean you are washing the soap itself. Also, soap is uncountable in English but in Korean a bar is counted, usually 비누 한 장 or 한 개.

Don't call liquid pump soap 비누; that pictures a hard bar. Use 물비누 or 핸드워시 for the pump bottle.
Don't count it as 비누 한 개만 always — a flat bar is naturally 한 장; 개 sounds fine but less idiomatic for a thin bar.

usage: to dry/wipe off with a towel
수건 ends in the consonant ㄴ, so the means particle is 으로
to wipe off the moisture with a towel
물기 = wetness/dampness; the standard thing a towel removes
flat cloth items are counted with 장
to hang up the towel (to dry)
널다 = to hang laundry out; the verb for drying a wet towel
examples: 수건이 젖었어요.
The towel is wet.
simple: 젖다 (to get wet) describes the state, with subject 이
샤워하고 수건으로 몸을 닦아요.
After a shower I dry off with a towel.
everyday: 닦다 here means to dry by wiping, not just to clean a surface
젖은 수건은 빨래통에 넣고 마른 수건을 꺼내요.
I put the wet towel in the laundry bin and take out a dry one.
real-situation: contrasts 젖은 (wet) vs 마른 (dry) modifiers on the same noun
nuance: 수건 is a cloth TOWEL for drying the body, hands, or hair, and its core collocation is 수건으로 닦다 — note 닦다 covers both 'wipe clean' and 'dry off', so 몸을 닦다 means dry yourself, not scrub. 수건 is Sino-Korean (手巾, 'hand-cloth'), which is why it feels slightly more everyday/native than the loanword 타월(towel); stores label big bath or beach towels 타월/배스타월, but in daily home talk 수건 covers everything. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first the particle — because 수건 ends in a consonant you must use 으로 (수건으로), not 로; second, don't reach for 말리다 here — you 수건으로 닦다 (wipe-dry with a towel), whereas 말리다 is for drying by air or a dryer (머리를 드라이기로 말리다).

Don't use 씻다 for drying off: 수건으로 씻어요 wrongly means 'wash with a towel.' Use 닦다 (수건으로 닦아요).
Don't count towels with 개 by reflex; a folded cloth towel is naturally 수건 한 장.

usage: to brush one's teeth with a toothbrush
칫솔 ends in ㄹ, so the means particle is 로 (ㄹ behaves like a vowel here)
모(毛) = hair/bristle; 칫솔모가 부드럽다 = the bristles are soft
the routine action of swapping an old brush for a new one
counted with the general counter 개
examples: 새 칫솔이에요.
It's a new toothbrush.
simple: 새 + noun = brand-new; here it just names the item
아침마다 칫솔로 이를 닦아요.
Every morning I brush my teeth with a toothbrush.
everyday: the full set phrase 칫솔로 이를 닦다; 마다 = every
칫솔모가 벌어지면 새것으로 바꿔야 해요.
When the bristles splay out, you should swap in a new one.
real-situation: 벌어지다 (to spread apart) is the natural verb for worn bristles
nuance: 칫솔 names the BRUSH itself, and you must keep three related words apart: 칫솔 = the brush, 치약 = the paste, and 양치(질) = the whole act of brushing/rinsing the mouth. The standard sentence is 칫솔로 이를 닦다 ('brush teeth with a toothbrush'); 이를 닦다 literally is 'wipe the teeth,' since 닦다 is the all-purpose verb for cleaning by rubbing. 칫솔 is a hybrid: 치(齒) is the hanja for 'tooth' (the ㅅ is the 사이시옷 inserted between 치 and 솔) and 솔 is native Korean for 'brush.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle after a ㄹ-final noun: ㄹ patterns with vowels, so it's 칫솔로, NOT 칫솔으로 — a very common beginner slip. Also don't say 칫솔질하다 for the daily routine; Koreans say 양치하다 or 이를 닦다.

Don't say 칫솔을 닦아요 to mean brushing your teeth; that means cleaning the brush. Say 칫솔로 이를 닦아요.

usage: 짜다 = to squeeze; the standard verb for getting paste out of the tube
to brush one's teeth with toothpaste
치약 ends in ㄱ (consonant), so the means particle is 으로
통 counts tubes/containers; a tube of paste is 한 통
to put toothpaste on the toothbrush
묻히다 = to apply onto; the natural verb for loading the brush
examples: 치약이 없어요.
There's no toothpaste.
simple: existence/availability with 없다, subject 이
칫솔에 치약을 조금만 짜요.
I squeeze just a little toothpaste onto the brush.
everyday: 짜다 (squeeze) + 조금만 (just a little); 에 marks where it lands
이 치약은 시린 이에 좋다고 해서 샀어요.
They say this toothpaste is good for sensitive teeth, so I bought it.
real-situation: 시린 이 = teeth that ache from cold; a common drugstore reason
nuance: 치약 is the PASTE you squeeze onto a 칫솔, and its signature verb is 짜다 (squeeze), not 누르다. Keep the trio straight: 칫솔 (brush) / 치약 (paste) / 양치 (the act). The hanja is transparent and worth remembering — 치(齒) 'tooth' + 약(藥) 'medicine/agent,' literally 'tooth medicine,' which is why it sounds natural to talk about a 치약 being '좋다' for some dental problem. It's counted by the tube: 치약 한 통 (or 한 개). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle pattern: 치약 ends in the consonant ㄱ, so the means form is 치약으로, never 치약로. A second trap is the verb — English 'put toothpaste on' becomes 치약을 묻히다/짜다, and 'brush with toothpaste' is 치약으로 양치하다; don't say 치약을 닦다, which would mean wiping the paste itself clean.

Don't say 치약을 누르다 for getting paste out; the idiomatic verb is 짜다 (치약을 짜다).

usage: to wash one's hair with shampoo
샴푸 ends in a vowel → 로; and hair takes the special verb 감다, not 씻다
떨어지다 here = to run out/be used up (a stock idiom)
헹구다 = to rinse with water; what you do after lathering
the partner products applied after 샴푸 (note Korean 린스 = English conditioner)
examples: 샴푸 냄새가 좋아요.
The shampoo smells nice.
simple: 냄새가 좋다 = smells good; here a noun-phrase comment
매일 저녁 샴푸로 머리를 감아요.
Every evening I wash my hair with shampoo.
everyday: locks in 샴푸로 + 머리를 감다 together
샴푸가 다 떨어져서 마트에서 새로 사 왔어요.
The shampoo ran out, so I went and bought a new one at the mart.
real-situation: 다 떨어지다 (completely run out) + 사 오다 (go buy and bring back)
nuance: 샴푸 is a loanword (from English 'shampoo'), so there's no hanja to parse, and it specifically means HAIR cleanser — its non-negotiable partner verb is 감다, the special Korean verb reserved for washing hair (and the head). The crucial contrast for a learner is exactly that verb: you 머리를 감다 (wash hair) but 몸을 씻다 (wash body) and 손을 씻다 (wash hands); using 씻다 with hair (머리를 씻다) sounds clearly off to natives. Watch a vocabulary false-friend too: Korean 린스 means CONDITIONER, not a 'rinse' — to rinse the suds out is the verb 헹구다. Because 샴푸 ends in a vowel, the means particle is 샴푸로 (not 으로). And note 떨어지다 doubles as 'fall' and 'run out,' so 샴푸가 떨어졌어요 means it's used up, not that it fell on the floor.

Don't write 샴푸으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 샴푸로.

usage: to look at oneself in the mirror
거울을 보다 = check your appearance, NOT stare at the glass
to be reflected in the mirror
비치다 = to be reflected; 에 marks the surface showing the reflection
깨지다 = to break (for glass); a natural everyday event verb
전신(全身) = whole body; the tall mirror you check your outfit in
examples: 거울이 정말 커요.
The mirror is really big.
simple: plain description with adjective 크다 and subject 이
아침에 거울을 보고 머리를 빗어요.
In the morning I look in the mirror and comb my hair.
everyday: 거울을 보다 = look at yourself, then 머리를 빗다
나가기 전에 전신 거울로 옷이 괜찮은지 봐요.
Before going out, I check in the full-length mirror whether my outfit is okay.
real-situation: 거울로 ... 보다 = use the mirror AS a tool to check; -는지 = whether
nuance: 거울 is a MIRROR, a native Korean word with no hanja to decompose, and its meaning hinges on a particle distinction English speakers miss. 거울을 보다 (object 을) idiomatically means 'look at yourself / check your reflection,' the everyday morning-routine sense — it does not mean staring at the slab of glass. By contrast 거울로 보다 (means 로) means 'use the mirror as a tool to see something,' e.g. checking behind you or your outfit. So the same noun flips sense with 을 vs 로. The reflection itself appears with 에: 거울에 비치다 ('be reflected in the mirror'). The pitfall: don't translate English 'look in the mirror' as 거울 안을 보다 ('look inside the mirror') — that's unnatural; the fixed phrase is simply 거울을 보다.

Don't use 보이다 when you mean 'I look at myself' — 거울을 보다 is active (you look); 거울에 비치다/보이다 is the reflection appearing.

usage: 휴지 ends in a vowel → 로; 닦다 = to wipe clean
칸 = a partition/square; the perforated section you tear off
to completely run out of toilet paper
떨어지다 = run out; the panic phrase in a stall
휴지 + 통(bin); the small trash can, often beside the toilet
examples: 휴지 좀 주세요.
Please pass me some tissue.
simple: 좀 softens the request; 주세요 = please give
화장실에 휴지가 없어요.
There's no toilet paper in the restroom.
everyday: existence with 없다, subject 가; the stall-emergency line
휴지로 입을 닦고 휴지통에 버렸어요.
I wiped my mouth with a tissue and threw it in the trash.
real-situation: shows 휴지 as table tissue + 휴지통 (bin) in one breath
nuance: 휴지 is the hanja word 休紙 — literally '休 rest/discard + 紙 paper,' i.e. 'paper to be used up and tossed' — and in real life it covers BOTH rolled toilet paper and the flat table tissue you wipe your mouth with; context tells you which. The contrast to learn is 휴지 vs 티슈 vs 화장지: 티슈 is the soft pop-up/pocket pack you carry, 화장지 is the more formal/printed label for toilet roll, and 휴지 is the broad everyday word. Note 휴지통 ('휴지 + bin') means the wastebasket, so don't picture only paper. The pitfall is the particle and the verb: you wipe WITH it, so 휴지로 닦다 (means 로, vowel-final), never 휴지를 닦다 (which would mean wiping the paper itself). Also 휴지 is uncountable-feeling but a torn square is 한 칸 and a roll is 한 통/한 롤.

Don't equate 휴지 only with toilet paper; it also means table tissue. The pocket pack you carry is 티슈.
Don't write 휴지으로; 휴지 ends in a vowel, so it's 휴지로.

usage: to wash one's face at the sink
에서 marks the place where the action happens; 세수 = washing the face
막히다 = to be blocked; water then 안 내려가다 (won't drain)
to wipe down / clean the sink
닦다 here = clean the surface; 를 marks the object cleaned
수도꼭지 = faucet; the spout fitted on the basin
examples: 세면대가 더러워요.
The sink is dirty.
simple: plain state with adjective 더럽다, subject 가
아침에 세면대에서 세수를 해요.
In the morning I wash my face at the sink.
everyday: 에서 = location of the activity; 세수하다 is the set verb
세면대가 막혀서 물이 안 내려가요.
The sink is clogged so the water won't drain.
real-situation: 막히다 + 안 내려가다 is exactly how Koreans report a blockage
nuance: 세면대 is specifically the BATHROOM wash basin where you clean your face and hands, and the sharpest contrast a learner needs is 세면대 vs 싱크대: 싱크대 is the KITCHEN sink for dishes, so the two are not interchangeable. The hanja is descriptive: 세(洗) 'wash' + 면(面) 'face' + 대(臺) 'stand/platform,' literally a 'face-washing stand' — which neatly explains why its home verb is 세수하다 (洗手, 'wash hands/face'). The natural particle is locational 에서 for the action done AT it (세면대에서 세수하다), and 가 when describing its state (세면대가 막히다). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly the 세면대/싱크대 mix-up, plus using 에 instead of 에서 — since washing is an action carried out there, it must be 세면대에서, not 세면대에.

Don't say 세면대에 세수해요; an action done at a place takes 에서 — 세면대에서 세수해요.
Don't use 씻다 for the face by itself; 'wash the face' has its own verb 세수하다 (or 얼굴을 씻다).

usage: to fill the bathtub with water
받다 here = to draw/collect water; 에 marks where the water goes
to soak (one's body) in the tub
담그다 = to immerse/soak; the verb for sinking into hot water
to take a bath in the tub
에서 = location of the activity; 목욕 = a soaking bath
반신(半身)욕 = soaking only the lower half; a common Korean tub habit
examples: 욕조가 커요.
The bathtub is big.
simple: plain description with 크다, subject 가
욕조에 따뜻한 물을 받아요.
I fill the bathtub with warm water.
everyday: 물을 받다 = draw water; 에 marks the destination
따뜻한 욕조에 몸을 담그면 하루 피로가 풀려요.
When I soak in the warm tub, the day's fatigue melts away.
real-situation: 몸을 담그다 + 피로가 풀리다 (fatigue is relieved)
nuance: 욕조 is the soaking BATHTUB, and the contrast that matters is the activity word: a long soak in the 욕조 is 목욕(하다), whereas a quick standing rinse is 샤워(하다) — many Korean apartments have only a 샤워 stall with no 욕조 at all, so this is a real cultural distinction, not just vocabulary. The hanja is 욕(浴) 'bathe' + 조(槽) 'tub/trough,' literally a 'bathing trough.' Its core verbs are 물을 받다 (fill it, lit. 'receive water'), 몸을 담그다 (soak/immerse), and the action takes locational 에서 (욕조에서 목욕하다). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping English 'fill the tub' onto the wrong verb — Korean says 욕조에 물을 받다, not 욕조를 채우다 in everyday speech — and confusing 목욕 (soak) with 샤워 (shower); 'take a bath' in a tub is 목욕하다, never 샤워하다.

mistakes: Don't say 샤워하다 for soaking in a tub; a tub bath is 목욕하다. 샤워 is a standing rinse.
Don't say 욕조를 채워요 in casual speech; the idiomatic phrase is 욕조에 물을 받아요.
Don't use 에 for the action of bathing; 'bathe in the tub' takes 에서 — 욕조에서 목욕해요.

usage: to comb one's hair with a comb
빗 ends in a consonant → 으로; the noun 빗 and verb 빗다 share a root
the everyday action verb, even when using a brush
-어 넘기다 = to sweep/push back; styling direction
참빗 = closely set teeth; 얼레빗 = widely set teeth
examples: 빗이 작아요.
The comb is small.
simple: plain description with 작다, subject 이
아침에 빗으로 머리를 빗어요.
In the morning I comb my hair with a comb.
everyday: noun 빗 + verb 빗다 together; note the 으로 after a consonant
엉킨 머리는 빗으로 천천히 빗어야 안 아파요.
Tangled hair you should comb slowly with a comb so it doesn't hurt.
real-situation: 엉키다 (get tangled) + 천천히 빗다 (comb slowly)
nuance: 빗 is a COMB, a native Korean word, and the neat thing learners must notice is that the noun 빗 and its action verb 빗다 (to comb) look and sound nearly identical — 빗으로 머리를 빗다 literally stacks 'comb-with hair comb,' which feels redundant in English but is perfectly natural in Korean. The near-synonym to separate is the tool type: 빗 is a flat comb, while a paddle/round HAIRBRUSH is 머리빗 or the loanword 브러시; in casual speech 빗 covers both, but a true brush is 브러시. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle after a consonant-final noun: it must be 빗으로, NOT 빗로 — and beginners often also drop the verb's irregularity, but 빗다 is regular (빗어요, 빗었어요). Don't say 머리를 솔질하다; the verb is simply 빗다.

Don't say 머리를 솔질해요 for combing; the verb is 빗다 — 머리를 빗어요.
Don't confuse the noun 빗 (comb) with 빚 (debt) — same sound, different spelling and meaning.

usage: 면도기 ends in a vowel → 로; 면도하다 = to shave (the action)
깎다 = to shave/trim; the verb pairing with 수염 (beard)
전기(電氣) + 면도기; the plug-in or rechargeable kind
날 = blade; the sharp part you replace when dull
examples: 면도기가 날카로워요.
The razor is sharp.
simple: state with 날카롭다, subject 가
아침마다 면도기로 면도를 해요.
Every morning I shave with a razor.
everyday: 면도기로 + 면도하다; 마다 = every
면도날이 무뎌져서 새 면도기로 바꿨어요.
The blade got dull, so I switched to a new razor.
real-situation: 무뎌지다 (become blunt) + 새것으로 바꾸다
nuance: 면도기 is the shaving TOOL, and the hanja explains its whole family: 면(面) 'face' + 도(刀) 'blade/knife' = 면도 ('face-blading' = shaving), plus 기(器) 'device' = the razor itself. So 면도하다 means 'to shave' and 면도기 is the instrument. The contrast to keep clear is 면도기 (the device) vs 면도 (the act) vs 면도날 (the replaceable blade), and an electric one is 전기면도기. Its partner verbs are 면도하다 (shave) and, with 수염 (beard), 깎다 (수염을 깎다, 'cut/shave the beard'). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle plus a doubled object: you shave WITH the razor, so it's 면도기로 면도하다 (means 로, vowel-final); never 면도기를 면도하다, which would absurdly mean 'shave the razor.' Also 면도기 ends in a vowel, so it's 로, not 으로.

mistakes: Don't say 면도기를 면도해요; you shave WITH it — 면도기로 면도해요 (or 면도기로 수염을 깎아요).
Don't write 면도기으로; it ends in a vowel, so the means form is 면도기로.
Don't confuse 면도기 (the razor) with 면도 (the act of shaving); 'do a shave' is 면도하다, the tool is 면도기.

usage: to dry one's hair with a hair dryer
드라이기 ends in a vowel → 로; 말리다 = to dry (something), transitive
to plug the dryer into the outlet
꽂다 = to plug/insert; 콘센트 = wall outlet
드라이하다 = to blow-dry (and lightly style) with the dryer
examples: 드라이기가 뜨거워요.
The hair dryer is hot.
simple: state with 뜨겁다, subject 가
샤워하고 드라이기로 머리를 말려요.
After a shower I dry my hair with a hair dryer.
everyday: 드라이기로 + 머리를 말리다; note transitive 말리다
드라이기가 고장 나서 머리가 안 말랐어요.
The hair dryer broke, so my hair didn't dry.
real-situation: contrasts transitive 말리다 (dry it) with intransitive 마르다 (it dries)
nuance: 드라이기 is the HAIR DRYER (from English 'dry' + the hanja 기 器 'device'); the fuller name 헤어드라이어 also appears in stores, and casual speech even uses just 드라이 (머리를 드라이하다 = blow-dry). Its essential partner verb is 말리다 (to dry something) — and here lies the single biggest English-speaker pitfall: 말리다 is the TRANSITIVE 'dry X,' while 마르다 is the INTRANSITIVE 'X dries / becomes dry.' So 드라이기로 머리를 말리다 = 'I dry my hair with the dryer,' but 머리가 마르다 = 'the hair dries (on its own).' Mixing them (e.g. 머리를 마르다) is ungrammatical. Because 드라이기 ends in a vowel, the means particle is 로 (드라이기로), not 으로. Don't confuse this with 다리미 (clothes iron) — both involve heat, but 드라이기 is for hair.
